lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: practical: investigate the effect of light on net gas exchange from a leaf, using hydrogen-carbonate indicator

primer.text: Hydrogen-carbonate indicator is a CO2 gauge you can read by colour. Four boiling tubes, four light treatments and a leaf apiece let you watch a plant's net exchange swing with the light — the daylight-darkness story of the previous notes, bottled and observable.

modules.title: Why Light Changes Net Exchange
sourceHeadings: Practical: The Effect of Light on Gas Exchange in Plants
modules.opening: The experiment compares leaves under four light regimes: full light, darkness behind foil, dim light behind muslin, and a control tube with no leaf at all. The indicator's colour law carries the information — yellow means carbon dioxide has accumulated above atmospheric levels, orange means atmospheric, purple means the leaf has drawn carbon dioxide below atmospheric levels.
keyPoints: The tubes compare photosynthesis and respiration under different light treatments.
Hydrogen-carbonate indicator turns yellow at high CO2, orange at atmospheric, purple at low.
Tube A holds no leaf and acts as the control in bright light.
Tube B sits in bright light, tube C is foil-wrapped for darkness, tube D wears muslin for dim light.
Each tube takes a fixed volume of indicator, bunged and left for hours or overnight.

low.restatement: Light decides whether the leaf drains carbon dioxide or fills the tube with it.
low.analogy: Four windows with different curtains: the room's temperature tells you which curtain was open.
low.examPointer: Memorise the colour scale in order — yellow, orange, purple — against rising, normal, falling CO2.

medium.restatement: Each tube isolates one light condition; the control isolates none at all.
medium.analogy: A line-up of suspects with one innocent bystander — the control — for comparison.
medium.examPointer: Name every tube's treatment when describing the setup; partial descriptions lose marks.

modules.title: Reading the Results
modules.opening: After hours or overnight the colours tell the story. The control stays orange. The bright-light leaf turns purple, because photosynthesis outruns respiration and drains carbon dioxide below atmospheric. The dark-wrapped leaf turns yellow, because respiration alone keeps feeding carbon dioxide into the sealed air. The dim-muslin leaf sits near balance: orange, or shading towards purple.
keyPoints: Tube A stays orange: no leaf, no change.
Tube B turns purple: photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so carbon dioxide falls below atmospheric.
Tube C turns yellow: respiration alone, so carbon dioxide climbs above atmospheric.
Tube D stays orange or turns slightly purple: the rates nearly balance.
Any change in tube D is far smaller than tube B's.

low.restatement: Purple means the leaf drained carbon dioxide; yellow means it filled the tube with it.
low.analogy: A bath with the plug half out: the water level's direction tells you which flow is winning.
low.examPointer: Attach a rate conclusion to every colour — photosynthesis greater, respiration greater, or balanced.

medium.restatement: Colour, then direction, then the rate verdict — the three-step reading.
medium.analogy: A thermometer reading that you then translate into hotter or colder weather.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing B, C and D conclusions in full sentences with the rate comparison.

modules.title: The Results Table and CORMS
sourceHeadings: The Effect of Light on Net Gas Exchange in Plants Table
Applying CORMS evaluation to practical work
modules.opening: A tidy write-up pairs every tube with its conditions, colours and conclusion — and the CORMS prompt checks the design itself: the Change is the light availability, the Organism is matched leaves, the Repeat guards reliability, the Measurements are the indicator's colour and the waiting time, and the Same list pins the indicator volume, leaf count and temperature.
keyPoints: The table maps each tube to conditions, initial colour, final colour and conclusion.
CORMS: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same — the design checklist.
The change here is the light treatment each tube receives.
Leaves should match in species, age and size across the tubes.
Repeats and fixed volumes make the comparison trustworthy.

low.restatement: The table records the results; CORMS audits the design that produced them.
low.analogy: A scoreboard plus a referee's checklist — one records, the other verifies fairness.
low.examPointer: Run CORMS aloud for any practical question; each letter is a mark opportunity.

medium.restatement: CORMS turns a good guess into a defensible design.
medium.analogy: Preflight checks before take-off: run the letters, then fly the experiment.
medium.examPointer: Write the Same list with three concrete items — volume, leaf count, temperature.

glossary.definition: A colour gauge for carbon dioxide: yellow at high, orange at atmospheric, purple at low levels.
The leaf-free tube establishing the indicator's unaltered colour.
The practical design checklist: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
